He believes he should always show respect to his parents and to older people. It is important to him to be obedient
Religious belief is important to him. He tries hard to do what his religion requires.
It's very important to him to help the people around him. He wants to care for their well-being.
He thinks it is important that every person in the world be treated equally. He believes everyone should have equal opportunities in life.
He thinks it's important to be interested in things. He likes to be curious and to try to understand all sorts of things.
He likes to take risks. He is always looking for adventures.
He seeks every chance he can to have fun. It is important to him to do things that give him pleasure.
Getting ahead in life is important to him. He strives to do better than others.
He always wants to be the one who makes the decisions. He likes to be the leader.
It is important to him that things be organized and clean. He really does not like things to be a mess.
It is important to him to always behave properly. He wants to avoid doing anything people would say is wrong.
He thinks it is best to do things in traditional ways. It is important to him to keep up the customs he has learned.
It is important to him to respond to the needs of others. He tries to support those he knows.
He believes all the worlds' people should live in harmony. Promoting peace among all groups in the world is important to him.
Thinking up new ideas and being creative is important to him. He likes to do things in his own original way.
He thinks it is important to do lots of different things in life. He always looks for new things to try.
He really wants to enjoy life. Having a good time is very important to him.
Being very successful is important to him. He likes to impress other people.
It is important to him to be in charge and tell others what to do. He wants people to do what he says.
Having a stable government is important to him. He is concerned that the social order be protected.
I work out what I think by talking it through with someone.
I prefer to form my thoughts privately before discussing them.
After a quiet day, I usually want some interaction with other people.
After an enjoyable social event, I usually want time on my own.
When I have a free afternoon, spending it with other people usually appeals to me.
I look forward to having an activity that I can enjoy on my own.
I tend to introduce a topic when a group conversation becomes quiet.
In a group conversation, I prefer to listen until I have something specific to add.
I like a day that includes frequent conversation.
I like long stretches of a day without conversation.
When both are available, I prefer discussing an idea live to exchanging written messages.
I find it easier to explore an idea when I can pause and reflect alone.
When I meet an unfamiliar problem, I first look for the broader pattern it might fit.
When learning something new, I prefer to begin with a concrete example.
An explanation interests me when it connects ideas that initially seem unrelated.
I trust an approach more when I can compare it with specific past experience.
I enjoy exploring possibilities before knowing whether they will be practical.
When someone describes an event, I want a clear account of what actually happened.
I tend to ask what a situation could become, beyond what it is now.
I prefer instructions that spell out the steps I can follow.
I usually want to understand the underlying principle before the details.
Specific observations are usually my starting point for making sense of a situation.
I find it natural to explain an unfamiliar idea by comparing it with a different subject.
I prefer descriptions that use literal examples over figurative comparisons.
When a decision affects several people, I begin by considering their individual circumstances.
When comparing options, I begin by defining criteria that apply equally to each one.
The effect a choice may have on a relationship is central to my decision.
I prefer to evaluate a proposal separately from my feelings about the person proposing it.
When a rule produces a difficult outcome for someone, I first consider whether the person's circumstances justify an exception.
When making an exception, I first consider whether I could apply the same reasoning to other cases.
When two workable options remain, I tend to favor the one that best reflects the values of the people affected.
When two workable options remain, I tend to favor the one that best meets the criteria agreed in advance.
When giving advice, I first explore what matters personally to the person asking.
When giving advice, I first map the likely consequences of the available options.
I find a decision hard to endorse if it conflicts with the personal values I bring to the situation.
I find a decision hard to endorse if its reasoning changes between otherwise similar cases.
For a shared activity, I prefer agreeing on a plan well before it begins.
For an open-ended task, I prefer deciding the next step as the work develops.
Once I have enough information for a workable choice, I prefer to settle it.
When there is time to decide, I prefer to keep several possibilities available.
I prefer knowing which tasks I intend to finish before I start the day.
I enjoy having room to change the order of my tasks during the day.
When arranging a trip, I prefer to settle the main details in advance.
On a day off, I prefer choosing activities as opportunities arise.
I like agreeing on a stopping point before starting a discussion.
I am comfortable leaving a plan unfinished while new information is still arriving.
Even when the stakes are low, I prefer having decisions settled.
I prefer arrangements that are easy to change when my interests shift.
